$comment: Decides which changes may merge without a human. Checked into the repo so the policy is reviewable, and read by classify-risk.py. Paths are fnmatch globs against repo-relative paths.
$principle: Fail closed. An unrecognised path is not automatically safe — it is judged by the default rule.
The question is never 'is this change good' (the gates answer that). It is 'if this change is
wrong, how bad is it, and can it be undone'. Anything hard to undo needs a human, however green.

rules.reason: Changes the thing that decides whether changes are safe. A run that can edit its own CI has no CI.

rules.$comment: stacks/** belongs here and was missing. Stack modules hold guard.json — twelve production deny rules across supabase and github, including the ones that stop a run reaching a remote database — plus this policy file and the classifier that reads it, plus deliver-run.sh. All of it was auto-mergeable, so a run could have deleted the rules protecting production and merged that change without anyone seeing it.
rules.reason: Guardrails and gate definitions. Same reasoning as CI config.

rules.$comment: The NOT NULL pattern used to match the words anywhere, so `CREATE TABLE ... body text NOT NULL` was held for review. A table being created has no rows, so a NOT NULL column on it cannot fail and locks nothing. The risk is adding a NOT NULL column to a table that already has data — ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL with no DEFAULT — which errors on any non-empty table and takes a rewrite lock where it does not. That is the property; NOT NULL by itself is just a column definition.
rules.reason: Irreversible or lock-taking schema change. Data removed by a migration is not recoverable from a green test suite.
Additive migration with no destructive statement. Auto-applies on merge; a snapshot is taken first.
Authorisation. A mistake here is silent, and the tests that would catch it are the ones most often missing.
Security headers and edge configuration. Weakening one is invisible in a diff review that is not looking for it.

rules.$comment: A lockfile has no contents that are not the dependency graph, so any change to one is a dependency change. This is the rule that does the real work — the package managers write the manifest and the lockfile together, so a dependency added by a tool rather than by hand is caught here even if the manifest rule below misses the shape.
rules.reason: A new dependency is the highest-consequence thing a run can add, and the thing a prompt-injected agent would most want to add.

rules.$comment: Held for review only when the added lines declare a dependency. A manifest also holds scripts, metadata, and tool config: editing `"test": "vitest"` in package.json was being held as if it added a package. The property that separates them is the value — a dependency's value is a version range, a script's is a shell command.
rules.reason: A new dependency is the highest-consequence thing a run can add, and the thing a prompt-injected agent would most want to add.
A manifest change that declares no dependency — scripts, metadata, tool configuration. The lockfile rule still holds anything a package manager installed.
Credential-adjacent. Should not appear in a run's diff at all.
Infrastructure. Failure modes are expensive and slow to reverse.
Money. A wrong amount or a double charge is not fixable by reverting the commit.

rules.$comment: `**/terms*` matched terms-editor.tsx — an admin component for editing the document, not the document. A prefix is not the property; being the published file is. So: the whole basename is the document name (terms.mdx, privacy.html), or it sits in a route directory of that name (app/terms/page.tsx). A component whose name merely begins with one of these words is ordinary code, and holding it taught everyone to wave the gate through.
rules.reason: Published claims and crawler policy. Wrong here is public before anyone notices.
